newsitem.title: JAPAN: Mazda 96/97 profit to rise, but group seen in red.
newsitem.headline: Mazda 96/97 profit to rise, but group seen in red.

text.p: Leading Japanese automaker Mazda Motor Corp is seen to have enjoyed solid profit growth last business year, thanks largely to the weak yen and sales of securities holdings, analysts said on Tuesday.

They expect Mazda's parent current profit for the year to March 1997 to be nine billion yen ($79.6 million) to 13 billion yen ($115 million), largely in line with the firm's estimate, but said it would stay in the red on a group basis.

The earnings, to be unveiled on Friday, would be a boost for Briton Henry Wallace, who took the wheel at Mazda in June after Ford Motor Co raised its holding in the carmaker to a one-third stake, giving it management control.

Wallace, in the spotlight as the first foreigner to run a major Japanese company, said last month that the company's financial structure and sales were improving, but he saw no surprises in its business results for 1996/97.

In November, Mazda saw its profit rising to 11 billion yen ($97.3 million) in 1996/97, nine times higher than the year before, when it marked its first profit in three years on sales of securities and painful cost-cutting.

But on a group basis, the nation's fifth-largest carmaker saw a net loss of four billion yen ($35.3 million) in 1996/97, staying in the red for the fourth consecutive year. Analysts said the loss would be bigger, around five billion yen ($44.2 million) to eight billion yen ($70.7 million).
Net profit is equal to current profit, which is pre-tax, minus taxes and extraordinary profits and losses.
Mazda is renowned for engineering expertise but has faced a shrinking market share since its strategy of becoming a niche maker of luxury cars and distinctive sports cars fizzled.

Analysts said robust sales of the new Demio compact car, launched last year, and the yen's weakness favoured Mazda's business last year. A dollar rise by one yen translates into five billion yen ($44.2 million) to six billion yen ($53.0 million) annual profits for Mazda, some said.
But analysts warned that the outlook is not rosy.

"It's too early to say that the business is on a full, good recovery, as it hinges on the sales of the new Capella model to be introduced later this year, and on the yen," said Seiji Sugiura, an analyst at Nomura Securities Co's research unit.
Sugiura, who saw a parent current profit of nine billion yen ($79.6 million) for 1996/97, said the profit could even slip to eight billion yen ($70.7 million) in the current year.
On a group basis, he saw a nil net profit this financial year as ongoing restructuring in the company's overall operations would continue to take a toll in the year.
Mazda last week announced that it planned to consolidate its loss-making North American operations, a move likely to lead to a 25 percent cut in its work force in North America.

Mazda said it would synchronise car production cycles and share common platforms with the parent company in a bid to cut costs. But it has not disclosed details such as how many platforms would be shared, for which models, or when the sharing would take place.
The two firms will share a number of car platforms, including engines and transmissions, but Wallace has said the real benefit from synergies with Ford will come beyond the year 2000.

On the company's share price, Sugiura said it may not fall from the current low levels, but uncertainties remain over how far it can rise due to a lack of details about the firm's planned synergies with Ford.
"We are still lacking factors to bid it up," he said.
On the Tokyo bourse, Mazda ended Tuesday's session down four yen at 345 yen. ($1=113 yen)
